items.output: This document specifies the retrieval component's ranking contract. The scorer accepts a query and a candidate set, and returns an ordering. Callers must not assume stability across versions; the ordering is defined only up to the documented tie-break rule. Two properties hold. First, monotonicity: if a candidate's relevance features strictly dominate another's, its rank is at least as high. Second, determinism: given identical inputs and a fixed model hash, the output ordering is byte-identical. Violations of either property are defects, not tuning opportunities. The contract deliberately says nothing about latency, which is governed by a separate service-level objective. Downstream consumers that require a probability rather than an ordinal should call the calibration endpoint; the raw scores are not calibrated and their absolute magnitudes carry no meaning. We state these constraints because past incidents traced to consumers reading structure into the scores that the contract never promised.
items.notes: No changes. This is precise technical writing. The formal register, the semicolons and the careful qualifiers (such as 'defined only up to the documented tie-break rule') are deliberate, and smoothing them would make the contract less exact.

items.output: This document specifies the retrieval component's ranking contract. The scorer accepts a query and a candidate set, and returns an ordering. Callers must not assume stability across versions; the ordering is defined only up to the documented tie-break rule. Two properties hold. First, monotonicity: if a candidate's relevance features strictly dominate another's, its rank is at least as high. Subject: Q3 churn rose 1.2 points, and we can't yet separate the causes

Hi all,

Monthly churn rose from 4.1% in Q2 to 5.3% in Q3, an increase of 1.2 points, or about 29% in relative terms.

We don't yet know why. Two events happened early in the quarter, the July 1 price change and the July 9 competitor launch. They are only eight days apart, and our analysis cannot separate their effects. I'd treat any claim that one of them explains the increase as premature.

One useful data point is that churn among annual-plan customers was unchanged at 1.2%. The increase is therefore coming from customers outside annual plans.

Next, we are surveying about 200 churned users to hear why they left. I expect results in mid-November and will follow up then with what they tell us about price versus the competitor.

Until then, I'd hold off on decisions that depend on which of the two is responsible. I can walk through the analysis if that would help.

Thanks,

*Incident summary for the DAU dashboard overstatement, Aug 4 to Aug 11*

*What happened*
A pipeline bug double-counted about 3.2% of events between Aug 4 and Aug 11.

*Impact*
- The bug overstated DAU dashboards by roughly 3% for that week. If you pulled numbers for Aug 4 to 11 before Aug 14, such as reports, exports, or slides, please refresh them.
- We retrained the forecast model on Aug 10 using the affected data, and we are still assessing the impact on the forecast. Please treat recent forecast outputs with caution until we report back.
- As far as we know, the bug did not affect any other models.

*Timeline and status*
- Aug 4 to 11: The pipeline double-counted events.
- Aug 10: We retrained the forecast model on the affected data.
- Aug 12: We fixed the bug.
- Aug 14: We completed the backfill, which corrected the affected week.
- Open: The forecast impact assessment is in progress.

*Next*
We'll share the forecast assessment as soon as it's done. If you see numbers for that week that don't look right, send them to us.

*Q4 demand forecast and recommended planning number*

*Summary*
The Q4 demand forecast is 118k units, with an 80% interval of 104k to 131k. You asked for a single number to plan against. I recommend 125k.

*Why not 118k*
118k is the most likely outcome, but it is not a safe planning number. Last year's Q4 forecast was off by 9%, which at this volume is roughly 10k units. The largest source of uncertainty this year is holiday timing. Thanksgiving falls late, which makes holiday demand harder to predict.

*Why 125k*
125k is in the upper part of the interval. It covers most plausible demand outcomes without planning for the 131k upper end.

The trade-off is that if demand comes in at the point forecast, we would hold about 7k more units than needed. Weighing that cost against the risk of a shortfall is a judgment call, and Supply is better placed to make it than I am.

*Next*
I will refresh the forecast on Nov 15 and tell you right away if the range or the recommended number changes.

*Fraud model v3 September holdout results and rollout plan*

v3 has higher precision and higher recall than v2 on the September holdout. Precision is 0.91 at recall 0.62, against 0.88 at 0.55 for v2.

I want to flag one regression. The false positive rate on new merchants is 2.1%, against 1.4% for v2, which is about 50% higher. We don't know why yet and are investigating.

*Plan*
- We will ship v3 to 10% of traffic on Monday.
- We will set a guardrail on the new-merchant false positive rate, so we catch this regression early in live traffic.
- We'll post what we find on the root cause.

If you know of anything that changed for new merchants, such as the onboarding flow, merchant mix, or data availability, please tell us. It could shorten the investigation.

Thanks to Priya for the feature work on v3.

*Onboarding survey summary*

*Headline*
61% of respondents said onboarding was confusing. The survey had 412 responses, an 18% response rate. The top themes in open-text answers were permissions setup and data import.

*How far to trust it*
Respondents skew toward power users. Seventy percent of them are weekly active, versus roughly 35% of users overall. Together with the 18% response rate, this means the sample is not representative, so the 61% may not generalize. From this data alone we can't say whether the true figure for all users is higher or lower. Less active users are underrepresented.

What the survey does tell us is that even in a sample weighted toward engaged users, a majority found onboarding confusing. The two themes also point to specific places to look.

*Recommendation*
Before redesigning, run about 5 follow-up interviews with new users. Focus the interviews on permissions setup and data import, and use them to check whether the survey's themes hold for people who are onboarding now.

*Email reminder experiment found no detectable effect on 7-day retention, so I recommend stopping*

The test found no detectable effect of the email reminder on 7-day retention. The estimate is +0.2pp (95% CI -0.5pp to +0.9pp).

The test was powered to detect a 1pp change. The top of the interval, +0.9pp, falls below that, so we can rule out a lift of 1pp or more. We cannot rule out a smaller effect, in either direction, within the interval. This is a result of no detectable effect, not proof of no effect.

*Recommendation*
Stop the test and don't ship the reminder. Any benefit is likely under 1pp, and we have no evidence that it is positive. Measuring a smaller effect would take a much larger sample, for a payoff that is modest at best.

*Incident update for the Oct 3 p95 latency spike*

*Status*
p95 latency rose from 340ms to 910ms, about 2.7x, starting at 14:12 UTC.

*What we know*
- The spike began 14 minutes after the 13:58 UTC config deploy.
- Traffic was also up 22% during that hour, so load is a possible contributor.

*What we don't know*
- The root cause is not confirmed. Our leading hypothesis is the cache eviction policy change in the deploy. We have not ruled out the traffic increase or other contributors.

*Next steps*
- We have scheduled a rollback of the deploy for 16:00 UTC.
- I'll post here after the rollback to say whether latency recovers. If it recovers, that supports the deploy as the cause, though we'll check against traffic at that time. If it doesn't, we'll widen the investigation.

items.output: Six months ago our on-call rotation was a mess. People dreaded their week, pages fired at 3am for things that could wait until morning, and nobody trusted the dashboards. We spent a quarter cleaning it up: deleted 40% of the alerts, rewrote the runbooks, and added a severity tier that actually maps to whether you should wake up. Last month we had two pages the entire rotation. The lesson for me was simple. Most alert fatigue is a design problem, not a discipline problem.
items.notes: No changes. The post is specific (3am pages, 40% of alerts deleted, two pages last month), and the closing line follows from that evidence. The "lesson" ending is a common LinkedIn shape, but here it is earned. If you want it tighter, you could drop "The lesson for me was simple."

We will not be able to fund everything, so rank ruthlessly and say what breaks if a line item is cut. Final decisions go out the first week of the quarter. Questions to me directly, not the group thread.

items.output: This document specifies the retrieval component's ranking contract. The scorer accepts a query and a candidate set, and returns an ordering. Callers must not assume stability across versions; the ordering is defined only up to the documented tie-break rule. Two properties hold. First, monotonicity: if a candidate's relevance features strictly dominate another's, its rank is at least as high. Second, determinism: given identical inputs and a fixed model hash, the output ordering is byte-identical. Violations of either property are defects, not tuning opportunities. The contract deliberately says nothing about latency, which is governed by a separate service-level objective. Downstream consumers that require a probability rather than an ordinal should call the calibration endpoint; the raw scores are not calibrated and their absolute magnitudes carry no meaning. We state these constraints because past incidents traced to consumers reading structure into the scores that the contract never promised.
items.notes: No changes. This is precise specification prose. The "First/Second" ordering, the "must not", and the "defects, not tuning opportunities" line are all doing real work in a contract, so I left them exactly as written.
